extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners and patent practitioners evaluating life-sciences claims
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for applying the Alice/Mayo subject‑matter eligibility framework to life‑sciences patent claims, including the markedly different characteristics and significantly more analyses for nature‑based products, diagnostics, treatments, and mixtures. Explains when to treat claim limitations as judicial exceptions and how additional elements or combinations can render claims eligible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 1 — statutory category (process/composition/etc.)
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether the claim recites a statutory category of invention (e.g., process, composition of matter, machine, manufacture).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the claim recites a statutory category (for example, 'a method of detecting JUL-1' is a process), proceed to analyze whether the claim is directed to a judicial exception. Example: 'The claim recites a series of steps ... Thus, the claim is directed to a process.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify whether claim is directed to a judicial exception
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether the claim (or claim limitation) is directed to a judicial exception such as a law of nature, natural phenomenon, product of nature, or abstract idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Point to the claim limitation(s) and explain why they constitute an exception (e.g., correlation between a biomarker and a disease is a law of nature; mental steps/critical thinking can be an abstract idea). Example guidance for rejections: 'identify step c as an exception by pointing to it in the claim and explaining why it is an exception, that the recited correlation is a law of nature ... and/or that the critical thinking step is an abstract idea.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Markedly different characteristics analysis for nature‑based products
rubrics_metrics.description: For claims reciting nature‑based products, evaluate whether the claimed product has 'markedly different characteristics' from its naturally occurring counterpart (changes in structure, function, or other characteristics).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider structural, functional, or other characteristic changes (e.g., granulation to defined particle sizes, addition of pectin to form a gel, altered organoleptic properties, encapsulation for controlled release). If the claim is focused on a process rather than the product, the markedly different characteristics analysis on recited nature‑based product limitations may not be necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI) to identify natural counterpart
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply the broadest reasonable interpretation of the claim to identify the appropriate naturally occurring counterpart for comparison.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: A claim to 'texiol and water' under BRI may cover the naturally occurring sap, so the analysis compares the claimed mixture to that naturally occurring material. Use BRI when determining whether the claim covers what exists in nature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Insignificant pre‑solution/data‑gathering activity
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether claimed additional steps are merely data‑gathering or other insignificant pre‑solution activity that do not add meaningful limitations beyond the exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High‑level steps such as 'obtaining a sample' or 'detecting using any generic antibody' are often well‑understood, routine, and conventional and count as insignificant pre‑solution activity (mere instruction to 'apply' the exception). Example: 'Obtaining a sample ... is well‑understood, routine and conventional ... amounts to insignificant presolution activity.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Physical/tangible element alone does not confer eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: The mere recitation of a physical or tangible element (e.g., a sample, a device, a step of administering a drug) does not automatically make a claim eligible if it is otherwise directed to an exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite Alice: 'the mere physical or tangible nature of additional elements ... does not automatically confer eligibility on a claim directed to an abstract idea.' Examiners should explain why physical elements are insufficient if they are routine or conventional.

rubrics_metrics.name: Significantly more — unconventional or particular application
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate whether additional element(s), alone or in combination, add 'significantly more' than the judicial exception by providing an unconventional step or confining the exception to a particular useful application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unconventional limitations (e.g., a coated microneedle array that is not a conventional delivery device; detecting with a porcine antibody when not previously used for human protein detection; using a specific antibody mAb‑D33; administering topical vitamin D where not previously used) can supply 'significantly more.' The limitation should be more than a mere instruction to 'apply' the exception using well‑understood, routine techniques.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combination of elements can provide significantly more
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider whether a new combination of steps or elements (even if individually conventional) integrates the exception into a practical application or improves a technical field, thereby amounting to significantly more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Diamond v. Diehr as precedent: 'a new combination of steps in a process may be patentable even though all the constituents ... were well known.' Example: combining accurate detection of a biomarker with a particular treatment to ensure proper diagnosis and treatment may integrate the exception into a diagnostic/treatment process and be enough for eligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conventionality is assessed at the time of filing
rubrics_metrics.description: When judging whether an element is conventional or routine, assess commonness and routine practice in the field at the time the invention was made and the application was filed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: topical vitamin D was not commonly used to treat julitis at filing time (unconventional), while administering anti‑TNF antibodies to treat julitis was well‑understood and routine at filing (conventional). Examiners must consider contemporaneous field practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: When to skip markedly different product analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: If the claim as a whole is focused on a process (practical application) rather than on a nature‑based product, it may not be necessary to perform the markedly different characteristics analysis on recited nature‑based product limitations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: claims directed to methods of treating or applying a product (e.g., administering antibodies to treat a disease) may be analyzed as processes, and examiners can focus on whether the process limitations recite a judicial exception rather than analyzing the product limitations' marked differences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Office action / reasons for allowance drafting guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: When issuing a rejection or reasons for allowance, identify the specific claim limitation(s) considered an exception and clearly explain why, and then explain why additional elements do or do not amount to significantly more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the record would benefit from clarification, add remarks to an Office action or reasons for allowance indicating the basis (e.g., that a peptide is a 'product of nature' because it 'lacks markedly different characteristics' or that a recited unconventional limitation confines the exception to a particular useful application). For rejections, 'identify the additional elements and explain why they do not amount to significantly more ... because they merely add data gathering and well‑understood, routine and conventional activities.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples of what counts as 'markedly different' or 'significantly more' (illustrative factors)
rubrics_metrics.description: Concrete factual indicia that can support finding markedly different characteristics or significantly more include: changes in organoleptic properties, controlled release behavior, defined particle size distribution (X10/X90), presence of non‑natural additives (e.g., pectin), use of a non‑conventional reagent (e.g., porcine antibody for human protein detection), and unconventional delivery devices (e.g., coated microneedle array).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the specification and factual record (e.g., sensory panels, known prior uses, prevalence in the field) to support findings. If evidence shows the recited formulation or reagent was not routinely used for the claimed purpose at filing, that supports eligibility.
